title: Paper Snowflake Start
challenge: Fold a square of paper into quarters, snip shapes along the folded edges, then unfold. Make six flakes and tape them to a window.
fact: The word Advent comes from the Latin adventus, meaning arrival or coming.

title: Secret Compliments
challenge: Each person writes three kind notes about a family member and slips them into that person's shoe or coat pocket to find.
fact: Poinsettias are named after Joel Poinsett, a U.S. diplomat who brought the plant from Mexico in the 1820s.

title: Trivia Showdown Night
challenge: After dinner, play Trivia Showdown on the TV. Teams of two, best of three rounds, and the winners pick the next game.
fact: Bing Crosby's 1942 recording of 'White Christmas' is one of the best-selling singles of all time.

title: Hot Cocoa Topping Bar
challenge: Set out cocoa, marshmallows, whipped cream, sprinkles and crushed candy canes. Everyone builds their own mug and names it.
fact: Wilson Bentley took the first known photograph of a snowflake in 1885.

title: Popcorn Garland
challenge: Pop a bowl of popcorn, then thread pieces onto string with a needle, alternating with dried cranberries. Drape it on the tree or a window.
fact: Snowflakes usually have six-fold symmetry because water molecules bond into hexagonal ice crystals.

title: Neighborhood Lights Walk
challenge: Bundle up and walk around the block to see the lights. Each person picks a favorite house and says why it stands out.
fact: The winter solstice is the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, around December 21 or 22.

title: Pictionary on the iPad
challenge: Play Pictionary on the iPad. Draw holiday words like sleigh, mitten, chimney, and snowman. Teams guess before the timer ends.
fact: Peppermint is a natural hybrid of watermint and spearmint.

title: Rainbow Paper Chains
challenge: Cut strips of colored paper, write one wish for the new year on each, and link them into a chain for the mantel.
fact: Rainbows form when sunlight is refracted and reflected inside raindrops.

title: Starlight Story Time
challenge: Turn off the lights, use a flashlight or string lights, and each person tells a short holiday story or favorite memory.
fact: Light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, takes about 4.2 years to reach Earth.

title: Would You Rather
challenge: Play Would You Rather on your phones. Each person sends in a holiday question, then everyone votes and explains their pick.
fact: 'Jingle Bells' was written in 1857 for Thanksgiving, not Christmas.

title: Frosty Sugar Cookies
challenge: Bake a tray of store-bought sugar cookie dough, cool them, and decorate with icing and sprinkles. Share a plate with a neighbor.
fact: Frost forms when water vapor turns directly into ice, skipping the liquid stage.

title: Holiday Treasure Chase
challenge: Hide small ornaments or wrapped candies around the house and run a treasure hunt with a timer. Count each find together.
fact: Aurora borealis is caused by charged particles from the Sun colliding with gases in Earth's atmosphere.

title: Name That Christmas Song
challenge: Play Name That Christmas Song with Alexa. Guess the title from the first few notes and keep score for the whole family.
fact: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was created in 1939 for a Montgomery Ward holiday booklet.

title: Comet Star Craft
challenge: Cut a star from cardboard, add a tail of tissue paper streamers, and hang it in a doorway or from the ceiling.
fact: Comet tails point away from the Sun, pushed by solar wind and sunlight.

title: Five Minutes of Calm
challenge: Sit together and breathe in for four counts and out for six for five minutes. Then each person shares one good moment from the week.
fact: Breath looks like a cloud in cold air because warm vapor condenses into tiny water droplets.

title: Wrapped Box Surprise
challenge: Wrap an empty box for a family member and fill it with handwritten coupons for chores, hugs, or picking the next movie.
fact: Galileo named the aurora after Aurora, the Roman goddess of dawn.

title: Sing-Along Carol Time
challenge: Sing along to a carol on the TV. Pick a song nobody in the family has sung this year and learn the first verse together.
fact: 'Silent Night' was first performed in 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria.

title: Pinecone Bird Feeders
challenge: Spread peanut butter on pinecones, roll them in birdseed, and hang them outside on string. Watch the birds from a window.
fact: Snow is made of ice crystals that form around tiny particles in clouds.

title: Coat and Toy Drive
challenge: Sort through toys, books, or coats you no longer use into a bag. Drop it at a local charity or shelter this week.
fact: The 1823 poem 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' named eight reindeer; Rudolph was added in 1939.

title: Blanket Fort Picnic
challenge: Build a blanket fort and have a picnic dinner inside. Play quiet games or read a book together by flashlight.
fact: Congress made December 25 a U.S. federal holiday in 1870.

title: Letter to Next December
challenge: Each person writes a short letter about this year and seals it to open next December. Keep the letters in a safe place.
fact: Emperor penguins huddle together in large groups during Antarctic winter to stay warm.

title: Card for Someone Alone
challenge: Make a handmade card for a neighbor, teacher, or relative who lives alone. Include one kind sentence and deliver it.
fact: 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' appeared as a poem by Jane Taylor in 1806.

title: Family Dance Party
challenge: Put on three favorite holiday songs and have a living room dance party. The last one still dancing picks the next song.
fact: Cacao beans were used as money in parts of Mesoamerica, including Aztec markets.

title: Christmas Eve Santa Watch
challenge: Check the Santa Tracker on the TV together. Then set out cookies and milk for Santa and a carrot for the reindeer.
fact: NORAD began tracking Santa in 1955 after a misprinted phone number in a newspaper ad.

title: Merry Christmas
challenge: Share one thing you love about each person in the family, then take a group photo in front of the tree. Merry Christmas!
fact: The word 'Christmas' comes from Old English 'Cristes maesse,' meaning Christ's Mass.
